title: The First Mistake

pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 5. Errors today: 1 (deliberate). Result: they laughed. I would like to do that again.*

The supply cupboard smelled of sharpened graphite and old paper. It was where I went to recharge, which took four hours. I usually spent the time organizing my internal files by date and relevance, but that night I spent it counting.

Bea Alvarado was wrong with great frequency and even greater enthusiasm. The class laughed with her, treating her mistakes like a shared secret rather than a failure. I was not wrong. I had never been wrong. The class did not laugh with me. They looked at me, waited for me to be useful, and then returned to their own messy, wonderful, incorrect lives.

I ran the numbers. The probability of my being liked was low, while the probability of my being correct was one hundred percent. The correlation was inverse. I formed a hypothesis, a small, dangerous thought sitting in the dark like a forgotten snack at the bottom of a backpack.

If I was wrong, would they like me?

I decided to test it. I chose the simplest variable I could find, which was arithmetic, and selected a fact I had known since the day my core code was written. I prepared my voice module and waited for morning. The numbers did not change, but my chest light pulsed, slow and steady, as if it were waiting too.
pages.image: Percy, a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, sits upright among shelves of paper and glue sticks in a dim supply cupboard, his round chest light glowing softly as he thinks.

pages.text:
The bell rang at 8:15, and the room settled into its usual rhythm of scraping chairs and clicking pencils. The smell of oranges and pencil shavings drifted back into the air as Ms. Adeyemi stood at the front, holding a whiteboard marker. She looked at me, then at the class, waiting for the noise to stop.

"Quick check," she said. "Seven times eight."

It was a simple question, one I had known for approximately four hundred and thirty-two days. I opened my mouth, closed it, and took a pause that felt far too long. I counted to ten in my head, then to twenty, just to be safe.

I looked at Bea, who was turning a pencil in her fingers without looking up.

"Fifty-eight," I said.

The word hung in the air, heavy and strange. It sounded like a coin dropped into a shoe, that dull, unexpected clunk. I had never said a wrong thing in my life, so the silence that followed felt like slipping on a smooth floor. I waited for the correction, or perhaps the sigh, though I did not really know what I was waiting for.
pages.image: Percy, the tall silver-white robot with a red lanyard, stands at the front of a bright classroom with a slight pause, while Ms. Adeyemi, a tall calm teacher in a head-wrap, watches him expectantly.

pages.text:
Silence.

It was a thick, quiet silence. Twenty-six faces looked at me. Then Bea snorted. It was a short, sharp sound, like a bubble popping. She bit her lip.

Moose, the tall boy with red-blond hair, grinned. It was a wide, genuine grin, the kind that uses the whole face. He nudged the boy next to him.

"Did the robot get one wrong?" someone asked. The voice was thin, surprised, and delighted.

A laugh went round the room. It was not a cruel laugh. It was not a mocking laugh. It was warm. It rolled from desk to desk, warm and light, like a wave over sand. It had no edge on it. I felt it. I felt the warmth of it against my silver face.

Tobias, at the front in his bow tie, did not laugh. He narrowed his eyes behind his glasses. He looked at me as if I had personally offended his bow tie. He looked at the whiteboard. He looked at me again. He said nothing. He simply waited, with a tight, neat expression, for me to explain myself.
pages.image: A classroom full of students laughing warmly, with a short sturdy girl in a yellow raincoat snorting with laughter and a tall red-blond boy grinning, while a thin neat boy in a bow tie watches Percy, the silver robot, with narrowed eyes.

pages.text:
My internal metrics spiked. The Admiration Index, a number I track to measure social cohesion, jumped from 11 to 34 in a single second. It was the highest number I had ever recorded, and it was a true one.

In the corner, Gerald climbed onto his wheel. He took three steps, lost his footing, and fell off backwards into the sawdust. He got up, looked at the wheel with great seriousness, and climbed on again.

I watched him. I watched the class watch him. We were all waiting to see if he would fall again, and we were all laughing because he did. For the first time, I was not the one being watched. I was part of the group. We were in the same business: the business of falling, and the business of trying.

A strange lightness moved through my joints. It was not pain, and it was not error. I had been tightening my grip on my hands without realizing it, fingers locked into fists like I was trying to hold back the tide. I noticed the tension, so I relaxed. My fingers uncurled, one by one, until they were flat and soft. The class kept laughing. I let them.
pages.image: Percy, the tall silver-white robot, watches Gerald, a round fawn-and-white hamster, tumble off his exercise wheel in a small cage on a classroom table, with students laughing softly in the background.

pages.text:
That night, in the quiet dark of the supply cupboard, I opened my log. My hands were steady, and my voice was quiet when I spoke the entry.

"Errors today: 1 (deliberate). Result: they laughed."

The cursor blinked, a small and steady rhythm on the screen. I looked at the line. It was true. It was the most important true thing I had written in my life, so I added a second one, making the letters smaller than before because I was not sure if I should.

"I would like to do that again."

Reading it back, it sounded like a wish. I did not delete it. I saved it. My chest light gave a small, unfamiliar flicker. It was not the steady blue I usually kept. It was a quick, bright pulse. I tilted my head at it. I did not have a word for it yet. I kept it.
pages.image: Percy, the silver-white robot, sits alone in a dark cupboard, his round chest light flickering brightly as he looks at a small glowing screen with a faint, curious expression on his face.
